---
title: "Performance and Validation"
---

## Performance is the product

Cellerator succeeds only when biological organization produces a measurable end-to-end advantage.

A representation is not successful because it is compact. A kernel is not successful because its isolated launch is fast. A planner is not successful because its decision is deterministic.

The relevant quantity is complete biological work.

## Evidence levels

### Level 0: hypothesis

A mechanism is plausible from access pattern, hardware behavior, or algorithmic analysis.

No performance claim is allowed.

### Level 1: microbenchmark

One primitive or kernel is measured with resident inputs.

The claim is limited to that primitive and shape.

### Level 2: operation benchmark

Projection construction, dynamic packing, kernel, epilogue, and output order are measured for one operation.

The claim covers that operation and reuse regime.

### Level 3: pipeline benchmark

Several operations execute with realistic order propagation, preparation, and synchronization.

The claim covers the complete pipeline.

### Level 4: application benchmark

A realistic biological or model workload is measured end to end, including data movement and repeated execution.

Only this level supports broad architectural claims.

Every result should state its evidence level.

## Required benchmark context

Record:

- repository commit;
- hardware model;
- GPU count and topology;
- compute capability;
- driver;
- CUDA runtime and toolkit;
- relevant library versions;
- compiler;
- build configuration;
- architecture flags;
- dtype and accumulation;
- input dimensions;
- structural distribution;
- output width `N`;
- expected reuse;
- warmup count;
- repeat count;
- synchronization method;
- included and excluded work;
- benchmark-mutex use;
- correctness tolerance;
- baseline versions.

## Complete cost accounting

For candidate \(k\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
T_k =&
T_{\text{host preparation}}
+
T_{\text{H2D}}
+
T_{\text{semantic packing}}
+
T_{\text{projection}} \\
&+
T_{\text{input order}}
+
T_{\text{persistent preprocessing}}
+
T_{\text{kernel}} \\
&+
T_{\text{epilogue}}
+
T_{\text{output order}}
+
T_{\text{communication}}
+
T_{\text{synchronization}}
+
T_{\text{D2H}}
\end{aligned}
\]

Not every term applies to every benchmark.

For repeated execution, report:

\[
T_{\text{amortized}}
=
\frac{
T_{\text{one-time construction}}
}{
R
}
+
T_{\text{per-run}}
\]

where \(R\) is reuse count.

Report the break-even reuse:

\[
R^*
=
\frac{
T_{\text{one-time construction}}
}{
T_{\text{baseline per run}}
-
T_{\text{optimized per run}}
}
\]

## Biological performance units

FLOPs are often not the useful denominator.

Report applicable metrics such as:

\[
\text{ns per useful edge}
=
\frac{T}{\text{active biological interactions}}
\]

\[
\text{bytes per useful edge}
=
\frac{\text{measured DRAM bytes}}
{\text{active biological interactions}}
\]

\[
\text{useful interactions per DRAM byte}
=
\frac{\text{active biological interactions}}
{\text{measured DRAM bytes}}
\]

\[
\text{descriptor efficiency}
=
\frac{\text{active interactions}}
{\text{descriptor-lane visits}}
\]

Additional domain-specific metrics include:

- ns per expressed gene;
- ns per active regulatory interaction;
- ns per motif hit consumed;
- bases read per downstream interaction;
- event bytes per effective regulatory interaction;
- active modules per launch;
- communication bytes per cross-partition edge;
- packing cost per reuse;
- useful cells processed per second.

## Hardware metrics

Collect the applicable subset:

- achieved DRAM bandwidth;
- L1 and L2 hit rate;
- global load and store transactions;
- sectors per useful interaction;
- warp execution efficiency;
- branch efficiency;
- issue and stall reasons;
- registers per thread;
- local-memory spill;
- shared-memory bytes;
- occupancy;
- eligible warps;
- atomics;
- launch count;
- host enqueue time;
- stream idle gaps;
- overlap of transfer, communication, and compute.

Use Nsight Systems for:

- launch trains;
- host gaps;
- synchronization;
- transfer;
- stream overlap;
- communication.

Use Nsight Compute for:

- hot-kernel memory traffic;
- occupancy;
- stalls;
- cache behavior;
- register pressure;
- warp efficiency.

## Baselines

Use the strongest relevant baseline.

Possible baselines include:

- cuSPARSE CSR;
- existing Cellerator CSR;
- SELL-C-sigma;
- BSR;
- Blocked-ELL;
- dense cuBLAS;
- current CP-BP row-masked tiles;
- alternate Cellerator projection;
- canonical-order graph;
- framework-native path;
- materialized Baseplane path;
- fused Baseplane path.

Do not compare only with:

- one launch per row;
- thousands of tiny copies;
- an intentionally unoptimized reference;
- a format known to be mismatched to the shape.

References may be slow. Performance baselines must be competitive.

## Current CP-BP evidence

The CP-BP v1 direct tile benchmark is valid evidence for one operation and a synthetic sharing spectrum.

It showed:

- high-sharing native tiles far ahead of CSR;
- medium-sharing native tiles ahead of CSR;
- low-sharing native tiles behind CSR;
- one launch and zero scratch for both native execution and its comparison path;
- no retained low-occupancy specialization.

This evidence supports hybrid dispatch.

It does not establish:

- large-`N` behavior;
- real-data generalization;
- sparse-to-dense ML performance;
- backward performance;
- a universal tile shape.

## Real-data structural corpus

Create a versioned corpus of structural traces.

Required sources should include examples from:

- scRNA-seq;
- scATAC-seq;
- paired multiome;
- enhancer-promoter relations;
- GRNs;
- pathway and module membership;
- cell-neighborhood graphs;
- developmental trajectories;
- sequence motif-to-element relations;
- sparse learned biological networks.

A trace may omit sensitive values while retaining:

- support;
- row and feature identities or anonymous stable surrogates;
- group structure;
- value-distribution summaries;
- operation profiles.

## Structural distributions to retain

For each trace, record:

- row-nnz distribution;
- feature-frequency distribution;
- partial-block occupancy;
- module overlap;
- support entropy;
- row similarity;
- feature similarity;
- hub frequency;
- rare-feature tail;
- rare-cell-state tail;
- cross-module edges;
- temporal stability;
- value magnitude and dynamic range;
- mutable versus static topology;
- expected operation widths;
- reuse horizon.

Synthetic generators should be fitted to these distributions, not invented only around convenient full blocks.

## Required `N` regimes

Benchmark at least:

```text
1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512
```

Also include non-power-of-two widths used by actual models.

## Adversarial corpus

Cellerator must test cases designed to defeat its preferred layouts.

### Random support

Uniform or near-uniform random sparsity with little reusable structure.

Expected outcome: native geometry should fall back rather than lose badly.

### Global hubs

A few features occur in almost every row.

Test whether:

- hub separation helps;
- cache reuse improves;
- metadata or synchronization dominates.

### Rare isolated features

Many features occur in one or a few rows.

Test residual representation and metadata overhead.

### Overlapping modules

Strong biological modules overlap so heavily that clean partitions create many cuts.

Test hierarchy and partition priors.

### Heavy-tailed rows

A small number of rows contain much more work.

Test dedicated heavy-row queues and load balance.

### Partial blocks

Feature blocks contain few active entries.

Test mask metadata versus padding and conventional sparse formats.

### Near-dense fragments

Density is high but just below the measured MMA break-even.

Test whether the planner avoids premature expansion.

### Rapidly changing topology

Structure changes too often to amortize packing.

Test a conventional or minimally prepared fallback.

### Forward-backward asymmetry

A forward geometry is excellent and its transpose is poor.

Test combined training cost.

### One-shot execution

Preparation and autotuning cannot amortize.

Test cheap analytical planning.

### Dense sequence hits

A predicate emits nearly every coordinate.

Test bit-plane and deterministic compaction paths.

### Sparse sequence hits

A predicate emits almost nothing.

Test atomic emit and fusion.

### Ambiguous sequence

Test validity, tail masking, and chunk halos.

### Distributed cut stress

Biological modules have many cross-GPU relations.

Test partition fallback and replication.

## Correctness before performance

Every optimized path must have:

- an independent reference;
- structural validation;
- randomized differential tests;
- adversarial dimensions;
- stale identity tests;
- capacity and offset tests;
- order round trips;
- projection equivalence;
- deterministic checks where promised;
- numerical tolerance defined by precision policy.

For GPU memory formats, run:

- Compute Sanitizer memcheck;
- racecheck where relevant;
- initcheck where useful;
- guard regions around inputs and outputs.

A sanitizer-clean aligned case does not prove an unaligned padded case.

## Numerical validation

Report:

- maximum absolute error;
- maximum relative error;
- mean error;
- distribution of error;
- task-level biological error where relevant;
- deterministic or nondeterministic behavior;
- accumulation order.

Quantization claims should include:

- calibration set;
- held-out set;
- scale granularity;
- outlier policy;
- saturation;
- impact on downstream biology or model metrics.

## Planner validation

A planner must be evaluated as a decision system.

Report:

- regret relative to the measured best candidate;
- candidate enumeration cost;
- analytical prediction error;
- autotune overhead;
- cache hit rate;
- stale-plan rejection;
- selection stability;
- performance across held-out structures;
- failure behavior in adversarial regimes.

A planner with low prediction error on the same regular synthetic generator is not validated.

## Conversion validation

For every projection or order transform, measure:

- construction time;
- bytes read and written;
- temporary memory;
- synchronization;
- device residency;
- break-even reuse;
- whether it can be persisted;
- whether it can be fused with producer or consumer.

The fastest kernel may lose after conversion.

## Graph validation

Compare:

```text
locally fastest kernels with canonicalization
```

against:

```text
graph-wide order-preserving plan
```

Record:

- total launches;
- total bytes;
- transform count;
- graph capture;
- end-to-end time.

## Baseplane validation

Sequence benchmarks must record:

- sequence length;
- motif or predicate;
- mismatch threshold;
- hit density;
- validity and ambiguity policy;
- output mode;
- output capacity;
- event order;
- H2D and D2H;
- materialized versus fused route;
- downstream interactions produced.

A fast predicate that creates an expensive unused event stream is not an end-to-end win.

## Multi-GPU validation

Record:

- partition axis;
- per-GPU work;
- boundary edges;
- replicated bytes;
- communication bytes;
- topology;
- collective or peer operations;
- overlap;
- imbalance;
- strong and weak scaling;
- local and global order transforms.

Compare biological partitioning with simple row ranges.

## Hardware generations

### Volta

Measure:

- manual cooperative staging;
- warp ballots and shuffles;
- WMMA fragments;
- register pressure;
- launch and HBM behavior.

### Ampere

Evaluate:

- asynchronous shared-memory copies;
- bf16 and newer Tensor Core modes;
- structured sparse hardware only where biology and measured cost support it.

### Hopper

Evaluate:

- TMA;
- warp-group matrix operations;
- producer-consumer specialization;
- thread-block clusters where cross-CTA reuse is real.

### Blackwell and later

Add architecture-specific implementations behind existing contracts. Do not change biological identity or semantic geometry merely to expose a new instruction.

## Benchmark mutex

All benchmark and profiler runs on shared hardware must serialize through:

- the repository benchmark mutex;
- active resource-reservation tooling;
- any workstream-specific GPU lock.

A result obtained while another worker uses the device is invalid unless contention is itself the experiment.

```text
Workload:
Biological interaction counted:

N:

Baseline:

Launches:
Synchronization:

Adversarial result:
```

## Rejection criteria

Reject a proposed optimization when:

- it wins only after excluding a required conversion;
- it loses at the expected reuse;
- memory expansion is unacceptable;
- a stronger existing baseline wins;
- the planner cannot identify its regime;
- correctness is weaker;
- it prevents graph capture without compensating benefit;
- it hard-codes one GPU generation into the semantic ABI;
- it adds metadata that costs more than the traffic it removes;
- it improves FLOPs while increasing time per useful biological interaction.

The performance program should be designed to kill weak ideas early. That is a feature.
